title: Midfield fight on a ‘knife’s edge’ as Audi target Haas
excerpt:
Nico Hulkenberg believes Audi must be “flawless” to capitalise on opportunities in the tightly contested midfield battle this weekend in Mexico, while team mate Gabriel Bortoleto remains confident the squad can close the gap to Haas in the teams' standings.

Audi head into the Mexico City Grand Prix looking to turn their recent competitiveness into valuable points, having narrowly missed out on the top 10 at the United States Grand Prix last weekend.

Hulkenberg recovered to finish 11th in Austin after an anti-stall issue at the start cost him several positions, while team mate Bortoleto climbed to 13th from the back of the grid following penalties for taking on new power unit components.

With Audi sitting eighth in the teams’ standings, seven points behind Haas, both drivers believe there are opportunities to make further progress in the remaining five rounds of the season.

Speaking on Thursday's media day in Mexico, Hulkenberg acknowledged that the increasingly competitive midfield leaves little room for error, with the German having finished 11th in three of the last four Grands Prix.

“I think we’re in striking distance, but we need to be flawless,” he said. “We need to be very clean, us drivers on the driving side and the team on the operational side, to really get those results.

“Otherwise, we’ll just be missing out. It’s really on a knife’s edge, usually with the Racing Bulls and the Alpines. So we go down to the wire, but it’s all to play for. The competition is high, and we’re ready for what’s to come.

"There is more on the table. Every weekend there are opportunities, and it’s our job to grab them and capitalise on them. I think our package is competitive, but we need to be clean and make no mistakes. The car needs to hold up... But if we stay clean, I think we’re in the fight for points.”

Bortoleto was similarly encouraged by Audi’s recent performance at the Circuit of The Americas, having shown top-10 pace throughout much of the weekend before his grid penalty left him facing an uphill battle on Sunday.

All the stories that got the Mexico City paddock talking

“Austin was very positive. Since FP1, I felt amazing with the car. We were inside the top 10 for most of the sessions,” said the Brazilian driver.

“We were super competitive. I felt so good when I finished that lap in Q1... At the same time, you leave the weekend believing there was an opportunity to be in the points, which we didn’t manage to achieve because of where I was starting. But it’s part of the game. We had to take the penalty, and now we move on. No penalty here, so hopefully I can have a good race.

“I’m looking forward to racing here. Last year, it gave me one point, so it’s a good track. Obviously, the long straights for us are a little bit of a pain, but we’re going to give our best. We’ll try to put in a good lap in Qualifying, have good pace in the race and hopefully deliver some points.

When asked about catching Haas in the Constructors' Championship, Bortoleto added: "We have five races to go, and we have good pace in most of these races. I think at some of them we may struggle a little bit more or less than at others, but I really believe we can achieve that."

title: The greatest pranks in Formula 1 history
excerpt:
Formula 1 drivers are used to keeping their rivals on their toes, but sometimes the biggest surprises happen away from the circuit. From team radio trickery to elaborate practical jokes years in the making, the paddock has never been short of mischief.

And while today's grid has plenty of pranksters, it is a tradition stretching back decades, with even some of the sport's greatest World Champions getting involved. With Halloween approaching, we revisit some of F1's most memorable practical jokes.

The team mates who just can't help themselves

Few Formula 1 partnerships have produced quite as many practical jokes as Ayrton Senna and Gerhard Berger's time together at McLaren between 1990 and 1992.

The Austrian was notorious for his mischievous sense of humour, and Senna frequently found himself on the receiving end. Their friendship produced several legendary stories, but perhaps the most memorable involved a trip to Australia, a hotel room and approximately 50 frogs.

After spotting frogs on a golf course during an evening run, Berger enlisted the help of a hotel concierge to collect them, reportedly handing over $100 for the favour. With the assistance of Ron Dennis' wife Lisa, Berger then scattered the frogs throughout Senna's room while the Brazilian was out at dinner.

When a furious Senna confronted his team mate the following morning, Berger had one more trick up his sleeve, asking if he had found the snake yet!

Fortunately for Senna, the snake didn't actually exist.

That wasn't the end of their antics, either. Berger also famously replaced Senna's passport photograph with an inappropriate image and once threw his supposedly indestructible briefcase out of a helicopter. Senna eventually retaliated by filling Berger's shoes with shaving foam.

Decades later, Ferrari teammates Charles Leclerc and Carlos Sainz developed their own entertaining partnership, although their pranks tended to be considerably less elaborate.

For Sainz' 28th birthday in September 2022, Leclerc spent around 15 minutes squeezed inside a cupboard in his team mate's driver room, waiting for the perfect opportunity to jump out and surprise him.

The plan worked, with an unsuspecting Sainz opening the cupboard to find Leclerc bursting out with confetti. Unfortunately, some of it also landed in the birthday boy's coffee.

At least Charles remembered his birthday!

When even the press conferences aren't safe

An FIA press conference might not seem like the obvious location for a practical joke, but Michael Schumacher and Sebastian Vettel proved otherwise at the 2012 German Grand Prix.

As Nico Rosberg attempted to answer a question, the two former World Champions noticed that his microphone was considerably louder than everyone else's.

Rather than alerting him to the problem, Schumacher encouraged Vettel to move Rosberg's microphone even closer to his mouth.

The result was an increasingly distorted answer as Rosberg spoke on, with the drivers around him struggling to contain their laughter.

And they weren't the only drivers to cause chaos during interviews. Following the 1999 Canadian Grand Prix, Eddie Irvine interrupted Mika Hakkinen's post-race interviews by throwing a towel at the McLaren driver, sparking an escalating exchange involving water.

Radio silence? Not quite...

There are few messages an engineer wants to hear less than a driver suddenly announcing an engine problem in the closing stages of a Grand Prix.

At the 2011 Japanese Grand Prix, Sergio Perez decided to use exactly that scenario for a joke.

The Sauber driver had started the race in 17th but produced an impressive recovery drive to climb into eighth, putting him on course for a valuable points finish. Then, on the final lap, Perez radioed his team to announce that he had no power.

His race engineer Marco Schupbach urged him to keep pushing towards the finish, only for Perez to reveal, after crossing the line, that the entire thing had been a joke.

Fortunately, Schupbach was quick to get his revenge!

The engineer told Perez that his teammate Kamui Kobayashi had finished fourth, despite actually crossing the line in 13th. The Mexican was completely taken in, repeatedly questioning the result before Schupbach revealed that he had been pranked in return.

And their practical jokes didn't stop there. Ahead of the 2012 Belgian Grand Prix, Schupbach enlisted the help of the Sauber team, including Kobayashi, for an elaborate revenge prank. Convincing Perez he was testing new wet-weather technology, they fitted a fake rain button to his steering wheel, leaving the Mexican puzzled by the supposed innovation. The entire encounter was secretly filmed, giving the team the last laugh nearly a year after his original radio prank.

Antonelli versus Bono: The Mercedes prank war

Kimi Antonelli might be fighting for the World Championship in 2026, but that hasn't stopped the Mercedes driver waging a rather different battle against his race engineer, Peter 'Bono' Bonnington.

It began during 2025 pre-season testing in Bahrain, when Antonelli celebrated Bono's birthday by pushing a plate of cream cake into his face. A year later, the Italian returned armed with a powerful water pistol, chasing his engineer through the paddock and even attracting the attention of Bono's former driver and seven-time World Champion, Lewis Hamilton.

Bono wasn't going down without a fight, threatening Antonelli with a fire extinguisher before getting his revenge by secretly adding hot sauce to the youngster's water bottle.

By May, Antonelli had taken his antics back to Mercedes HQ in Brackley, arranging for Bono's security pass to be deactivated. When the engineer found himself locked out, he immediately suspected the culprit to be the young Italian!

The tables eventually turned at the Italian Grand Prix in September, when a group of Mercedes mechanics ambushed Antonelli with plates of whipped cream to celebrate his 20th birthday, some wearing protective ponchos for the occasion.

But there is one person Antonelli hasn't dared to prank just yet – Team Principal Toto Wolff. Speaking in October, the Italian admitted that targeting his boss would require considerably more courage, but a successful championship campaign might finally give him an excuse!

A seat at the table for George Russell

When the drivers gathered for their traditional end-of-season dinner ahead of the 2024 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, tensions between Max Verstappen and George Russell were already making headlines.

After the pair clashed during the previous race weekend in Qatar, the rest of the grid spotted an opportunity for some entertainment.

Naturally, the rest of the grid spotted an opportunity for some entertainment.

As Liam Lawson later explained on an F1 podcast, the drivers deliberately filled the seats around the dinner table while keeping a place free beside Verstappen for the late-arriving Russell.

When Russell finally appeared, Verstappen cheerfully informed him that they had saved him a seat!

Unfortunately for the pranksters, Russell wasn't prepared to play along. Rather than take the offered spot, he simply picked up the chair, carried it to the opposite end of the table and sat alongside his then-Mercedes teammate Lewis Hamilton.

Lawson later admitted the group had found the entire situation hilarious, even if their intended victim hadn't been quite so amused!

An ear-resistible prank

Returning to the scene of his 1976 Nurburgring accident might have seemed an unlikely setting for a practical joke, but Niki Lauda had other ideas.

In 2013, ahead of the release of Rush, the film depicting his rivalry with James Hunt, Lauda returned to the Nurburgring with an American television crew.

As the three-time World Champion discussed his infamous 1976 accident, in which he suffered severe burns and injuries, he suddenly bent down and retrieved something lying in the grass.

Holding it up, Lauda jokingly announced that he had discovered his missing ear.

The horrified reaction was exactly what he had hoped for. The object was actually a biscuit that Lauda had discreetly placed on the ground beforehand, allowing him to turn a serious interview into an unforgettable practical joke.

The next generation of paddock pranksters

The 2026 grid has provided its own share of practical jokes, particularly at Racing Bulls, where Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad have been getting creative with their attempts to embarrass one another.

In October, Lawson teamed up with Sky Sports F1 presenters Simon Lazenby and Naomi Schiff to trick his rookie team mate into taking part in a staged television interview, completely unaware that the whole thing had been arranged as a prank.

But Lindblad soon had his revenge. With the help of a hidden earpiece, he turned Lawson into an unsuspecting participant in a series of challenges around the paddock, directing his team mate through the experience and putting him in some rather uncomfortable situations, including stealing Charles Leclerc’s microphone mid-interview.

And the McLaren drivers aren't immune to a little mischief either. During a media day karting challenge at Silverstone in July, Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri took control of a two-person kart, with Norris operating the pedals and Piastri steering.

But after the challenge ended, Norris decided to accelerate away with his unsuspecting team mate still aboard, leaving Piastri unable to do much other than hold on for the ride, even losing his hat in the process.

More than three decades after Berger was sneaking frogs into Senna's hotel room, F1's tradition of practical jokes is still going strong.

And with Halloween approaching, a few drivers might want to keep an especially close eye on their team mates...

title: Sauber veteran Zehnder to leave Audi at end of 2026
excerpt:
Veteran Swiss engineer and long-time Sauber Team Manager Beat Zehnder will leave the Formula 1 team now known as Audi at the end of the year.

The 60-year-old joined Sauber Motorsport in 1988, five years before the operation entered Formula 1, and won the 24 Hours of Le Mans and World Sportscar Championship with Sauber's sportscar programme.

He was there on the first day the Formula 1 team opened its doors in 1993 and stepped up to Team Manager the following year before being appointed to the management committee in 2018.

The Swiss worked on 601 consecutive Grands Prix and will have spent nearly four decades with the Hinwil-based squad.

During his time at the team, he has worked with the likes of world champions Kimi Raikkonen and Sebastian Vettel, plus race winners Charles Leclerc, Sergio Perez, Robert Kubica, Felipe Massa and Heinz-Harald Frentzen.

When Audi made Sauber their works team, he moved into a factory-based role, leading Audi's heritage activities as Director of Signature Programs and Operations.

On Friday, ahead of the Mexican Grand Prix weekend, Audi said Zehnder will leave the organisation "following the restructuring of its operations ahead of the 2027 season".

They added: "Beat has been a mentor to hundreds of team members and drivers who have passed through Hinwil over the years.

"During his tenure, he enjoyed both the highs and lows of working in such a demanding sport, never losing his professionalism, his relentless competitive streak and desire to win.

"We thank him for 39 years of outstanding service and wish him all the very best for the future."

title: Bearman offers update on F1 future ahead of Mexico City GP
excerpt:
Ollie Bearman has confirmed ahead of this weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix that "it's very clear I want to continue with Haas" in 2027, although no official announcement has yet been made.

Earlier this month Haas confirmed that Esteban Ocon would be replaced by Ferrari junior and current Formula 2 points leader Rafael Camara, the Brazilian expected to partner Bearman.

But Bearman's future has yet to be announced, with the Briton coming to the end of his second season with the American outfit.

"I think it's very clear I want to continue with Haas and that's definitely my goal," said Bearman during Thursday's media day in Mexico City.

"There's a few things in the background that we're working on but it's been very clear that continuing with Haas will be my target and we're just finalising a few things on that front."

When asked when any announcement would be coming, Bearman replied: "I don't know to be honest.

"It's not really in my hands, I can tell you that. If it was up to me, it would already have been announced a long time ago but there are a few bigger picture things that we're working on."

Bearman sits P13 in the drivers' standings, 16 points clear of Ocon, and arriving at a venue this weekend where he claimed his best finish in F1 with a fourth place.

Having lost his seat for 2027, Ocon confirmed in Mexico that discussions were still ongoing with a view to keeping him on the grid, with the second seat at Cadillac alongside Sergio Perez a possible option.

"I'm not going to really comment on the discussions I've had with teams in general," said Ocon when asked about the Cadillac rumours.

"Of course, we are talking with a lot of people on the grid at the moment. I feel like I have unfinished business in F1. I'm still very young, I still have a lot of things to achieve and that's where I want to be in the future."

title: Hadjar identifies the ‘weakness’ Red Bull still suffer from
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar believes that Red Bull need to work on improving their starts after a slow getaway hindered their performance at the United States Grand Prix, with the Frenchman “still a bit frustrated” by the result.

After matching his best-ever Qualifying of P3 in Austin, Hadjar dropped down the order on the opening lap and felt that “everything went wrong” as he suffered a throttle problem before settling for P6 at the chequered flag.

It was the latest in a run of challenging rounds for the 22-year-old, who missed out on a podium in Sepang due to a battery issue and endured a difficult weekend in Singapore as technical problems limited him to a P10 finish.

Hadjar was nevertheless satisfied with Red Bull’s underlying pace, as he explained ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix: “I’m still a bit frustrated about [Austin] because I came back from such a tough weekend, where I was really struggling out there in free practice, to fighting for pole and having great pace on Sunday.

“We struggled a bit with a few issues, radio-wise. I was blocked on something, which was quite frustrating to drive with, and the start was not nice.

“There have been a couple of things that compromised us, but the main important one, raw pace, was just great. I’m just happy about that.”

His team mate Max Verstappen has demonstrated that Red Bull have what it takes to win races, having triumphed in both Malaysia and Singapore, which has left Hadjar optimistic that they can secure another strong result in Mexico.

Elaborating on their starts and his expectations, he added: “There have been times when we’ve thought, ‘Oh, we’ve got this under control,’ and then it went back in the other direction. Austin was one of those weekends. I can’t guarantee anything, but I know we’ll push hard.

“There’s nothing that could be done in the last couple of days. We go with what we have, and in the past we’ve managed some good ones. We want to replicate that, and we’ll push through until the end.

“We’re aware of the weakness – we need better starts. We need better radio quality because it’s a bit difficult to do a race without that. And the pace was, I must say, very strong. We’re happy about that.

“But now Mexico is a completely different challenge. It’s a track that’s so slippery, you’re just sliding around so much. It’s not the most enjoyable, but it’s a great layout so let’s see.

“I’ll just try to adapt. If we can minimise the damage, I’m happy. At the start, it’s also a long run down to Turn 1. We can get a nice tow, and that can help for sure.”

title: Why Sergio Perez means so much to Mexico
excerpt:
There are few places where Sergio Perez’s popularity is as obvious as the Autodromo Hermanos Rodríguez. And this weekend, as Mexico City celebrates its Grand Prix alongside Día de Muertos, the home favourite returns to mark another milestone: his 300th Grand Prix.

When Checo leaves the pit lane, it will be his 10th home race and his first in Cadillac colours. Results have been hard to come by for F1’s newest team, but that is unlikely to diminish the reception for a driver who has become one of Mexico’s biggest motorsport figures.

The sound of home

When Perez arrives at the Autodromo, attention follows him everywhere. Inside the Foro Sol, the old baseball stadium incorporated into the circuit, the reception can be deafening. Checo has said himself that he can hear the crowd and feel the cheers from the cockpit.

In 2021, racing alongside Max Verstappen at Red Bull, he finished third to become the first Mexican driver to stand on the podium at his home Grand Prix. He ended up wrapped in the flag while the whole Foro Sol chanted his name.

A year later, he was third again, before the heartbreak of 2023, when a first-lap collision with Charles Leclerc ended his race. Now at Cadillac, a home podium may be a long shot, but his supporters are no less committed.

EXCLUSIVE: Sergio Perez reflects on his F1 career in photos

From Guadalajara to his 300th race in F1

Perez's career has taken him around the world, but it is rooted in Mexico. Some time ago, on a kart track in Guadalajara, a six-year-old Checo was often the youngest in his class but never the slowest.

At 14, he headed for Germany to race in Formula BMW, alone in a country that was nothing like home. Homesickness hit hard, but he decided to give his career everything, convinced that going home would mean never leaving again.

Within a decade, he became the first Mexican on the F1 grid in over 30 years, following in the footsteps of Pedro and Ricardo Rodriguez, the brothers after whom the Mexico City circuit is named.

Making history for Mexico

Perez made his F1 debut with Sauber in 2011, becoming the first Mexican driver on the grid in more than 30 years. After spells with McLaren, Force India and Racing Point, his breakthrough victory finally came at the 2020 Sakhir Grand Prix.

Now after a year out, he’s with Cadillac, signed until at least the end of 2029, and heading home to look back on every step that led to this 300th race.

Five more wins followed with Red Bull, making him the most successful Mexican driver in F1 history, while he also twice stood on the podium at his home Grand Prix. Alongside Max Verstappen, he helped Red Bull secure back-to-back Teams’ Championships.

A hero beyond the circuit

Mexico’s affection for Perez stretches far beyond the circuit. His image has become part of the landscape, painted on walls from Mexico City to Nuevo Leon as a reflection of the pride surrounding the country’s most successful F1 driver.

At the entrance to the Autodromo Hermanos Rodríguez, artist Duek Glez has immortalised Checo in graffiti, while in Mexico City’s Roma Norte neighbourhood, muralist Yim Miyaki marked his return with a painting carrying the message “Checo races with Mexico”. Further north, in San Nicolas de los Garza, artists Claudio Robledo Mtanous and Dariana Vazquez Guajardo have also celebrated the Mexican driver through their work.

But Perez’s influence extends beyond the murals bearing his image. His success has helped bring more Mexican fans to F1 and inspired greater interest in motorsport in a country where, for a generation, he has been its most visible figure on the world stage.

Back where he belongs

This weekend brings the thin air of the highest circuit on the calendar, the roar of the Foro Sol and, on Sunday, a landmark for a national hero.

Perez has acknowledged that returning home in a developing Cadillac, without the expectation of fighting at the front, presents a different challenge to his Red Bull years. But the reception awaiting him says something about his relationship with Mexico.

For a decade, Checo’s home Grand Prix has been about far more than where he finishes.

title: All the stories that got the Mexico City paddock talking
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli touched down in Mexico earlier this week knowing that he stands on the brink of becoming Formula 1's youngest World Champion following a beautifully crafted victory last Sunday in Austin.

However, we didn't get to hear from him on Thursday in the Mexico City paddock, as the Mercedes racer was under the weather while recovering from a viral illness.

The 20-year-old stayed at the hotel after being given dispensation to miss his mandatory media duties at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.

title: Why Tsolov has complicated Racing Bulls’ 2027 plans
excerpt:
Nikola Tsolov’s FP1 appearance for Racing Bulls in Mexico has put a further spotlight on the driver log jam in the Red Bull camp.

A frontrunner in F2 this year who has already logged F1 mileage through TPC running at Imola, Tsolov would ordinarily be primed for a Racing Bulls race seat in 2027.

The fact that in recent years Isack Hadjar, Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad all took part in FP1 sessions in Mexico indicates that it’s a rite of passage of sorts.

Indeed, a few weeks ago Racing Bulls Team Principal Alan Permane made it clear that there is a three-into-two scenario, confirming that Tsolov is very much in the frame.

The challenge for Red Bull’s management is that all three of the aforementioned drivers have performed superbly this season, and with Hadjar already confirmed alongside Max Verstappen at Red Bull there won’t be any changes at the senior team.

As the only rookie in the 2026 field, Lindblad has impressed, and from the outside it seems obvious that his job isn’t under threat. The Briton is relaxed about waiting for firm news.

“In the end, I'm just focused on my year and doing as best as I can,” said Lindblad. “I know that's the thing that's going to help me. Always, when performance is better, that helps.

“Honestly, it's not something I've wasted too much energy on. I've been part of Red Bull for a long time. I'm very much part of this family. So it's not something that I'm wasting much energy on.”

Lawson’s case isn’t so clear cut. At the start of this season most observers would have assumed that his long-term future was uncertain, and that he would be the obvious man to be dropped should Red Bull promote a youngster.

The New Zealander has made life more difficult for his bosses by not only regularly making Q3 and scoring points with Racing Bulls, but also by doing a solid job when he subbed for the injured Hadjar at the senior team. Dropping him now would be a harsh decision, to say the least.

“I just feel like it's been a very strong year for us,” he explained. “And especially the second half, things have been very, very strong. And trying to find that consistency in F1 is very, very hard, and it can go away from you very quickly.

“And with how many variables there are, it's obviously something that's always a factor, but for us, I think we've maximised really a lot this year, especially the second half.

“I'm not really sure much what more is expected, but I'm also not really sitting there thinking too much about the whole seat selection thing. A year ago I thought about it a lot, it was very much in my head. And you just drive worse – you just overthink things.

“So this year I feel like I haven't really thought about it much at all. And things have been strong, so I'm just trying to keep that keep that mindset up, trying to score as many points as I can in the season.”

Whatever happens, at least Lawson knows that he’s done the best job he can.

“That's the biggest thing as a driver,” he said. “You come away from a weekend sometimes, and even if you can't score points, I think the biggest thing is personally you want to be able to walk away and feel like you've done everything you can. And if you've done that, that's a satisfying feeling.

“Well it can be at least. It's more satisfying than if you don't, if you make a mistake or something like that. There are always things you can do better, and I'm sure looking over the year, there's a lot of things to tidy up.

“But overall, I feel like I've done a very strong season, and if I wasn't driving next year, I would feel like there wasn't much more that I could have done.”

Ultimately the key to his survival in a race seat could be those races he did for Red Bull. The traditional purpose of the Faenza team has always been to provide drivers to the senior outfit, and thus those who were no longer felt to be potential graduates have generally been dropped.

After the disappointment of 2025, Lawson seized his second chance at the Milton Keynes team.

“There was a lot of talk over the last 12 months after I left Red Bull that that maybe I wasn't a driver that could be good enough to drive in Red Bull, because of my start,” he said.

“And it's not really something I spoke too much about, but going back to the start of 2025, we did half a day in Jerez before the season, we had a compromised Bahrain test, and we had Melbourne where we missed P3 with an engine issue, and then China was a Sprint, and that was it.

“So versus this year, I feel like obviously having a lot more experience going into Red Bull this year, maybe if there's one thing I take from it, it's that at least I could show people that I can drive that car – or any car.”

title: Norris defends McLaren's progress ahead of Mexico City GP
excerpt:
Lando Norris has defended McLaren's 2026 development progress ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix, and believes that the team have "had a pretty good year" after a tough start to the campaign.

The reigning World Champions suffered a slow start under the new ruleset, which included a double Did Not Start for Norris and McLaren team mate Oscar Piastri in China.

The team have made steady progress during the season, which culminated in Norris taking back-to-back wins in Hungary and the Netherlands, while a third victory in Madrid was denied due to an ill-timed Virtual Safety Car.

Although McLaren have fallen away from the front of the pack in recent races due to a difficult handling car, Norris is proud of the work achieved by the team so far.

"The car has been horrible and difficult to drive the whole season, just other teams have brought a lot more upgrades since and improved a lot more than what we have. Nothing more than that," said Norris during Thursday's media day in Mexico City.

"The team is still doing a good job, considering we were almost one and a half seconds off at the beginning of the year, one second off. The fact we even won almost three races was a pretty sizeable achievement in itself.

"So I think we’ve had a pretty good year, if we want to look at it from that perspective. Of course, we hold ourselves to a very high level, and we want to win everything we can.

"We started a long way behind at the beginning of the season, and we’ve done a good job to catch up. We’ve done better than the majority of other teams on the grid."

McLaren sit equal on points with Red Bull for P3 in the teams' standings, with two victories for Max Verstappen in recent races proving pivotal.

Piastri believes that staying ahead of Red Bull will prove difficult over the remainder of 2026 – with McLaren's focus already on 2027 – but remains hopeful.

"You just have to keep fighting. I think at the moment we know we’re not as competitive consistently as Red Bull are, but we’re adding performance to the car still, and there’s a lot of things that can happen," said Piastri.

"Reliability has been a big topic this year, so there’s still plenty of ways it can turn. But clearly, on pure performance, we need to make some steps forward, and we do still have some things coming to the car that’ll hopefully help with that.

"I think for us, it’s going to be a big challenge to stay ahead of Red Bull, but we’re always up for it."

title: ‘I don’t care’ about the Drivers’ Championship – Verstappen
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has insisted that he doesn’t “really care” about the fight for second place in the Drivers’ Championship and would rather focus on improving Red Bull’s challenger for 2027.

Recent results have demonstrated that the Milton Keynes-based outfit should never be written off – after a frustrating wait for victories, Verstappen marginally missed out in Azerbaijan before clinching consecutive wins in Malaysia and Singapore.

Their resurgence has propelled the Dutchman up the standings, where he now sits just six points behind George Russell in P2 and five adrift of third-placed Lewis Hamilton, while Red Bull are also level on points with McLaren.

Asked ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix how important a strong finish in the Drivers’ Championship would be, Verstappen replied: “I don’t really care, because it’s only about first. So for me, I don’t care if I’m second or fifth.

“The only thing that we want to try and achieve is to be P3 in the Constructors’. That’s what I think the team wants, so that’s what we’ll try to do.”

Although Red Bull haven’t finished outside of the top three in the Teams’ Championship since 2015, Verstappen went on to explain that his biggest priority is ensuring that they begin next season with as strong a car as possible.

“[There are] still a lot of things that we want to change, and I hope that it will bring the car a bit more together,” he said. “That’s been the target already for a long time.

“Of course, we have improved a lot this year, but I think we are nowhere near satisfied enough, so there will still be a decent amount of changes for next year.”

Verstappen has won at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez five times in his career, but Red Bull’s struggles last time out in Austin – where he was unable to hold off Charles Leclerc for P2 – left him reluctant to expect another triumph.

“There were a few little issues that we found, which of course we were dealing with throughout the weekend,” he explained. “So it’s more about trying to learn from them, trying to fix them and trying to have a little bit more of a straightforward race.

“It’s not the same track, so it’s a very different scenario. It’s very hard to say. Of course, if we fix or know how to fix some of the things that we had in Austin, naturally your pace is better. It’s very simple.

“I had a bit of damage on my car. Some other bits were not where we wanted them to be, and from the engine side, it was not where we wanted it to be operating and performing, also in terms of horsepower.

“So a lot of little things that contribute to lap time lost. If you fix that, you naturally pick up pace. We know that if the car and engine are in better shape, then you should go faster. But here, there are so many different elements that come in that it’s very hard to predict whether suddenly you’re fighting for the win again or not.”

title: The 10 F1 rookies who will drive during Mexico City FP1
excerpt:
The opening practice session of the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend will feature 10 rookies during the 60-minute outing.

As per Article B1.7.3 of the sporting regulations, F1 teams are required to provide two practice outings per car during the season to give experience to rookie drivers.

The Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez has proven to be a popular location to do so this year, with Ferrari being the only squad not to nominate a substitute for the opening practice segment.

At the front of the field, Fred Vesti will once again jump behind the wheel, standing in for George Russell in what will be his seventh FP1 appearance.

Reigning Formula 2 champion Leonardo Fornaroli will climb aboard the McLaren for the third time this year, while Ayumu Iwasa will have another appearance at Red Bull.

There will be three FP1 debutants on Friday - Nikola Tsolov for Racing Bulls, Freddie Slater for Audi and Gabriele Mini for Alpine.

Luke Browning will have another outing with Williams, while Jak Crawford and Ryo Hirakawa will fulfil duties at Aston Martin and Haas, respectively.

Finally, Colton Herta is having another go at Cadillac, and depending on his mileage during the session, he could finally be eligible to pick up a super licence required to race in F1.

title: Max Verstappen clarifies 'average' comment after painful race
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has offered clarity on the “average” comment he made after the United States Grand Prix last weekend.

The Dutchman finished the race in third place, marking his sixth consecutive podium result.

However, he was unable to secure his third win on the bounce, having prevailed at the two rounds prior in Malaysia and Singapore.

Verstappen delivered an “average” verdict after the race when assessing the performance of the car, but has now moved to further define what he meant by the comment.

“I didn't say it was average on that track compared to other tracks, what I said was average is that we are not the quickest in the low speed and we are not the quickest in the high speed,” Verstappen told media including RacingNews365.

“That means that our car is probably sitting a little bit in the middle over all of these corners.

“On some tracks, that's all right and then on some tracks, probably it's a little bit more limiting.

“That's what I meant with average.”

[Article continues below]

Verstappen highlights importance of low speed corners in Mexico

Verstappen enters the race weekend in Mexico targeting his sixth win at the venue, which would set a new personal record for the most wins at one track.

But with a unique environment existing due to the high altitude in the city, Verstappen stated that the low-speed performance will be crucial due to the reduced downforce.

“We have to see here, it's a lot less grip with the altitude,” he said.

“Normally, we have the wings to compensate a little bit for that, but now you basically just run one wing.

“So it will be a lot less downforce on the car, which I think will already be quite challenging.

“That probably puts even more emphasis on low-speed performance.”

title: Carlos Sainz bites back at Fernando Alonso 'low quality' drivers criticism
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz has issued a defence of the driving standards towards the back of the F1 grid following fierce criticism from Fernando Alonso.

At the United States Grand Prix last weekend, Alonso was involved in an opening lap incident with Sainz's team-mate Alex Albon.

After the race, Alonso stated that the "quality of the drivers in the low third of the grid is very low" in an apparent jab at the Williams driver he collided with.

Sainz has rejected the criticism from his compatriot, insisting he holds Albon, who is currently in his seventh season in F1, to a high standard.

"[It was] a bit harsh towards Alex," Sainz told media including RacingNews365. "I think he [Alonso] was referencing more towards him [Albon].

"I really rate Alex very highly, and he's a guy that I enjoy racing with, and never shown any disrespect or bad moments with him.

"Also, Fernando, I have fun battling with him. I've never been in the last third of the grid until this year.

"All my life I've been having a car to battle for the points, at least in my Toro Rosso days, Renault, McLaren, always top 10.

"It's the first time in my career I find myself battling in the back end of the midfield."

[Article continues below]

Current F1 grid 'the best one' - Sainz

Like Alonso, Sainz has been relegated towards the rear of the field this year as Williams failed to deliver at the start of the new regulation cycle.

Having now spent time fighting for positions further down the order, Sainz further refuted Alonso's statement by claiming the current grid is the most talented he has ever seen in F1.

"I've been on the grid 12 years, and if there is one year that I think is the highest level of talent on the grid, it's this one," he said.

"I can't think of anyone who is not up to F1 standards. All the rookies that have come in over the last few years are good.

"Some make mistakes, like I used to do when I was younger, and I still do mistakes now, you've seen me do [them] this year.

"In the last half of the grid there are more incidents, but I prefer to think it's circumstantial and not because of the quality of the grid."

title: Lewis Hamilton predicts 'unusual experience' as F1 drivers set for Mexico challenge
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton is hoping to get in the fight at the fight at the front of the field this weekend in Mexico.

Lewis Hamilton has stated the downforce limitations in Mexico this weekend will result in an "unusual experience" for the drivers.

The F1 cars this year have had downforce slashed compared to 2025 as part of the new technical regulations in play.

The effect is set to be even more obvious this weekend in Mexico City, whose high altitude creates a unique environment for the drivers to compete in.

Due to the low air density, less downforce is generated compared to other locations on the F1 calendar.

Hamilton is expecting that the drivers will have a much different experience behind the wheel p compared to F1's last visit to Mexico City 12 months ago.

"Someone just said that it's going to be good for our car, but I really have no idea," Hamilton told media including RacingNews365.

"Everyone is going to be max downforce here. It will be an unusual experience for us all, because it's like 25 or 30 per cent less downforce than we had the last time we drove here, or even in Monza, for example."

[Article continues below]

Driver

Lewis Hamilton

Hamilton thinks Ferrari car 'should be good' in Mexico

Hamilton has not enjoyed a positive experience behind the wheel of late, scoring just one podium in the last nine races.

Team-mate Charles Leclerc has bagged two runner-up finishes at the last two events, highlighting the existing potential in the Ferrari car.

While Hamilton has not had an easy time in recent rounds, the seven-time champion is confident it can compete towards the front this weekend.

"So whether we can get the tyre switched on, I think the car should be good here.

"Being that we have [high] altitude, hopefully straight-line speed won't be as affected as it is on some of the other places where, at sea level, the drag is significant.

"I'm hoping that we are able to continue on the strong performance that we had last year and bring it into this weekend."

title: Charles Leclerc unsure of 'short-term' Ferrari fix as 'limitation' revealed
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has admitted Ferrari may not have a "short-term" answer to the sensitivity that cost the team a potential front row in Austin, with the Monegasque identifying keeping the SF-26 in its "right window" as a current "limitation".

Leclerc qualified fourth at Circuit of the Americas despite having been a favourite for pole position, with Ferrari's strong pace across practice suddenly disappearing come the final part of qualifying/

Starting from fourth ended Leclerc's realistic hopes of victory in Austin, although a strong start allowed him to fight for a podium and finish second.

Now, Leclerc enters the Mexico City Grand Prix where Ferrari are again tipped to perform strongly, to the extent that the Scuderia has been deemed by some as favourites.

Speaking to select media including RacingNews365 ahead of the weekend in Mexico, Leclerc was asked whether Ferrari arrive as the team to beat.

"I don't know," said Leclerc. "Honestly, I think it's getting very close, and we have good momentum. With Singapore and Austin as well, we've maximised our potential, and I was relatively happy with the pace we've shown.

"Whether we are the favourites for this weekend, I don't fully agree. I think Mercedes remain the favourites wherever we go. Red Bull are very, very strong as well recently. But if we maximise everything we have, then I hope it can be a great weekend for us.

"As we've seen, I think the optimisation of our package is what will eventually make the most difference. It's so difficult to put everything in the right window coming into qualifying that, if we manage to do so, I think we've got a chance here."

Leclerc then turned to why qualifying in Texas proved so difficult, pointing to a specific weakness that reared its head when track temperatures dropped late in the session.

As a result, he is unsure whether Ferrari's key area of struggle will reappear this weekend in Mexico City.

"I mean, we've got a strong car, but it's a car that is very sensitive whenever we get off the optimum window," Leclerc began explaining.

"We've paid the price a little bit recently in Q3, particularly when the track temperatures are going down. Then we just struggle a bit more compared to the others to keep everything in the right window.

"That's what happened in Austin, unfortunately, in the lap that counted the most out of Friday and Saturday. Eventually, we lost a front row because of that. It's a limitation we know about and that we're focused on. Whether we have the solution in the short term, I'm not sure.

"But at least it's a point of focus and something we'll make sure to try to get as right as possible coming into Saturday here."

title: Isack Hadjar makes 'on fire' prediction as F1 braced for extreme test
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar has predicted that every part of an F1 car will be "on fire" during this weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix.

At 2,285m above sea level, the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez is the highest circuit F1 visits, with the air density around 25% lower than at sea level.

As there is less air going into the car, the brakes often overheat in Mexico, with cars also generally running extreme engine cooling louvres to try and force as much of the scant air through the intakes to cool critical areas.

In a further complication, the turbos are going to have to work harder in 2026 than in 2025 as the MGU-H has been removed from the power units.

The component aided the turbo by allowing it to spool up to faster RPMs, thus eliminating turbo lag and providing instant power response when demanded by the throttle, but with the overhaul for the new engines, the part was eliminated to simplify the designs.

As such, the turbos will be worked harder with less air available, which will increase temperatures inside the engine - as Hadjar spoke of the "extreme" challenges drivers will face.

"I'm just thinking about how extreme it's going to drive these cars," Hadjar pondered to media, including RacingNews365.

"Like last year, already it felt like sliding around a lot with the Monaco rear wing, and now it's kind of the same downforce level throughout the year, and you're going on a track like that.

"It's going to feel slippery, like hell, so, of course, there are extreme conditions for the car, cooling-wise.

"It's going to be very extreme, and for the engine as well, for the tyres, for the brakes. I mean, just everything is going to be on fire, even myself in the car probably.

"So, I'm not thinking about Ferrari or Mercedes. I think, of course, they are going to be very competitive.

"I'm mostly thinking about how tough on our end the weekend is going to be, but in the last couple of races, the car's been working well on all very different kinds of tracks, so why not here?"

[Article continues below]

Hadjar's response to Austin comments

The Frenchman was then also asked about his comments following the United States Grand Prix, in which he claimed Red Bull was incapable of doing the "stupid little things" right following clutch and radio issues at Austin.

"We'll keep pushing, and it's something we've been working on, and there have definitely been big improvements if you look at the first couple of races of the year, and now we're at a point where it goes a bit up and down," Hadjar said when presented with his comments from Austin.

"We are aware of that, and we need to work with what we have until the end of the year. But the good thing is, the tough thing of going fast on track, I think we're doing it.

"I think we also got it a bit wrong on the strategy. It's been reviewed; we move forward, but I wouldn't say they are silly things. I would say they are important little things that we don't do."

Turning to the Austin strategy itself, Hadjar then declared that the team wasn't "open-minded enough" to attempt a one-stop.

"We were probably not open-minded enough to the one-stop strategy, and we were very convinced the soft compound was working better, and maybe we thought the deg was higher than it actually was," he said.

"And once you start with this, then we put ourselves in a difficult situation because I had a good pace on the soft; I didn't want to pit too early. At the same time, we don't want Max to lose his race time because he's on another strategy.

"So, in the end, that was confusing because if in the end, if we were all on a one-stop, everyone would have been happy."

Summing up his response to Austin, Hadjar conceded that there was "stuff I should have kept to myself for sure" about his criticism.

title: Lando Norris shares 'funky' advice as two F1 drivers suffer Mexico illness
excerpt:
Lando Norris has explained how he avoids "funky foods" and uses "bottled water" to avoid illness in Mexico, as two F1 drivers missed media day.

Kimi Antonelli, who will be crowned champion after Sunday's race if nearest rivals George Russell or Lewis Hamilton don't win the race, was given permission by the FIA to miss speaking to the media after contracting what Mercedes called a "viral illness."

Cadillac driver Valtteri Bottas was also then excused from his duties for feeling unwell.

The final 12 races of the season, from the Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort on August 23rd to the planned finale in Abu Dhabi on December 6th are in a 15-week run, with four triple-headers broken up by one weekend off.

These triple-headers are spread across Europe, Southeast Asia and Eastern Europe, and the Americas, with the final three races planned as a triple-header for Las Vegas-Qatar-Abu Dhabi, although the final two races are still uncertain given the ongoing crisis in the Middle East.

Norris, who is into his eighth season of F1, spoke of how he tries to avoid falling ill and the steps he takes as the championship crisscrosses the planet.

"I'm pretty simple, so I try to avoid all of the funky foods," Norris explained to media, including RacingNews365, when asked about how he copes with travelling late in the season.

"I keep sticking to pasta; I just stick to pasta and a bit of chicken every now and then.

"Here [in Mexico], I don't have any tap water. I brush my teeth with bottled water and all that stuff, so it is simple things.

"I've been ill here in the past and the same in Brazil, so I guess over time, things become a little more predictable, and you know what to avoid.

"Luckily, as I'm quite fussy with my food, I avoid a lot of the stuff that can make me ill, but I also just rest.

"I have Monday and Tuesday off, just to myself to not do anything, and you don't realise it, but even marketing days just drain you a lot.

"I don't have a lot of time to recover, even though it is just talking and thinking about things all day, but when you're racing, when you're travelling, you need a good rest."

[Article continues below]

Norris's travel arrangements

The outgoing champion also spoke of his preference for arriving early in countries to adapt and rest before races.

"It is just sleeping, getting to places on time, and a lot of people travel out very late," he said of his preparations.

"I prefer travelling out very early to places, so everyone has their own way of doing things."

title: Audi announce exit of major team figure after 39 years of service
excerpt:
Audi has confirmed that Beat Zehnder will leave the outfit at the end of December 2026, bringing the curtain down on a 39-year association with the Hinwil operation.

The departure comes as part of a restructuring of the team's operations ahead of the 2027 season.

Zehnder joined Sauber Motorsport back in 1988 and was part of the squad's sportscar programme, which won the 24 Hours of Le Mans and the World Sportscar Championship in both 1989 and 1990.

He moved into Formula 1 with the team in 1993, before being named team manager the following year, a role he held for more than two decades.

Zehnder was appointed to the Management Committee in 2018 and, most recently, led the team's Heritage activities as Director Signature Programs & Operations.

Over his near four-decade stint at Hinwil, Zehnder worked with many names, mentoring such high-profile drivers as Kimi Raikkonen, Felipe Massa, Sebastian Vettel, Robert Kubica and Charles Leclerc.

He leaves with 36 World Sportscar Championship races and 601 consecutive Formula 1 races to his name.

The team thanked Zehnder for his service, highlighting that throughout his tenure, Zehnder never lost his “professionalism, his relentless competitive streak or his desire to win.”

title: Max Verstappen makes striking F1 prediction about Kimi Antonelli
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has insisted Kimi Antonelli will get “even better” as a driver as he sits on the verge of a maiden world championship.

The 20-year-old enters the Mexico City Grand Prix this weekend needing only a ninth-place result in the race to clinch the title.

Antonelli's meteoric rise to the height of F1 success has come in just his second season, having made a substantial step forward after a challenging rookie campaign.

With nine wins in his pocket so far this year, Verstappen predicted that Antonelli will only mould himself into a sharper driver after he wins his first title.

“He hasn’t yet tapped into 100 per cent of his potential, and winning the world title will make him even better,” Verstappen told Bild

“You’ve achieved your life’s goal and start approaching race weekends with a more relaxed attitude.”

In the same discussion, Verstappen also discussed one of the grid's oldest drivers, seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton.

Verstappen highlighted that a significant difference between Hamilton and Antonelli is the fact that the latter can still get faster as a driver due to his inexperience.

“He [Hamilton] probably won’t get any faster," Verstappen said.

"Don’t get me wrong: I’m not saying Lewis is getting slower, just that he won’t get any faster. It’s different with Kimi. There’s still a lot more left in him.”

title: Dakar Rally confirms new 2027 host after move away from Saudi Arabia
excerpt:
The Dakar Rally will move to Europe and Africa for its 49th edition in 2027, organisers have confirmed, following recent events in Saudi Arabia.

The race will be hosted across Portugal and Morocco before returning to Saudi soil in 2028 for its 50th edition. The Dakar Classic, Dakar Future Mission 1000 and Dakar Saudi Next Gen programme will follow the same shift.

The news comes just several days after the FIA confirmed the 2027 Dakar Rally would not take place in Saudi Arabia amid the ongoing crisis in the region.

The 2027 season-opener for the FIA and FIM World Rally-Raid Championships will run from 9-23 January, pending approval from the FIA's World Motor Sport Council, comprising a prologue and twelve stages between Loulé-Faro and Marrakech.

The Algarve will stage the prologue and opening special stage, before competitors cross the Mediterranean to Morocco, which will host eleven stages and a rest day in Agadir. The route covers 7,824km, including 4,341km of special stages, across six bivouacs.

Dakar director David Castera described the challenge of putting together the route at short notice.

"The relocated 49th edition of the Dakar will meet the sporting standards that have always made it the most demanding rally-raid event,” he said.

“Despite the short timeframe we have had to work with, we have designed a true Dakar.

"The ACP (Automóvel Club de Portugal) is supporting us in Portugal, having established its round of the FIA-FIM World Rally-Raid Championship as a cornerstone of the season since 2024.

“And in Morocco, our expertise across the entire territory, combined with the operational capabilities of our internal teams, allows us to go far beyond the formats previously offered in the country: competitors will discover the Kingdom from one end to the other.

"We are already grateful for the loyalty of the competitors who are overwhelmingly choosing to follow us on this new adventure (350 already registered to date).

"The adventure continues, as do preparations for the historic celebration of the 50th edition in Saudi Arabia."

title: F1 drivers set to follow MotoGP lead: 'Definitely something to discuss'
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has confirmed that the F1 drivers are set to follow the lead of their MotoGP counterparts and discuss any concerns over racing in the Middle East for the final two grands prix of the season.

Ahead of last weekend's race at Phillip Island in Australia, which was eventually cancelled due to severe weather and poor visibility that prevented the medical helicopters from operating safely, the 22 riders staged a rare meeting amongst themselves to discuss the issues of racing in Qatar next weekend.

It is understood that, given the growing uncertainty in the region due to the looming threat of an escalation in the war between Iran and the United States, the riders expressed serious concerns about their safety and those of their teams.

Further meetings have followed in the build-up to this Sunday's race in Sepang, Malaysia, between the riders and their team managers, and then with MotoGP CEO Carmelo Ezpeleta.

Those willing to discuss the matter with the media chose their words carefully. Yamaha rider Alex Rins stated: “I would like to talk [more] about it, but I can't. The only thing that I can say is we are really united, all the riders, more than ever."

At this stage, MotoGP has not made an official announcement, which, like F1, is run by the same commercial rights holder, Liberty Media.

Asked whether similar conversations had taken place amongst the drivers ahead of F1's visit to Qatar in four weeks, followed by Abu Dhabi to conclude the season a week later, Ferrari driver Charles Leclerc said: "It's definitely something that I think will come up in the talks.

"We haven't necessarily talked about it too much through the GPDA [Grand Prix Drivers' Association], but it's definitely a topic that will probably be on the list of things that we need to discuss. We'll see what happens."

[Article continues below]

Perez - 'Things can change from day to day'

Speaking in the FIA press conference ahead of this weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix, home hero Sergio Perez felt that the MotoGP riders were right to discuss the matter.

"Nobody knows at the moment," said Cadillac driver Perez on the possibility of racing in the Middle East. "It can change from one day to another. Things can ramp up.

"At the moment, it looks like the right thing from what we've seen in MotoGP, but I just think these things can change day to day."

Naturally highlighting the fact the final decision is out of the drivers' hands, he added: "We're not the ones taking the decisions. The people who take the decisions will obviously have full responsibility for them, so it's not really for us to say much on it."

Williams driver Alex Albon agreed it was a "wait and see" situation. He added: "There are still quite a few weeks ahead of us.

"It is obviously a sensitive area. Looking at the MotoGP side of things, I think the riders are doing the right things in getting the insurance assurances they're asking for."

title: George Russell handed brutal verdict as F1 season spiral continuation tipped
excerpt:
George Russell has been handed a damning verdict from RacingNews365 readers, with a poll on who will finish second in the 2026 drivers' championship suggesting fans expect his recent slump to run through to the end of the season.

Asked to predict the runner-up behind championship leader Kimi Antonelli, just 2.7 per cent of voters backed Russell, despite the Briton currently sitting second in the standings on 242 points.

Max Verstappen dominated the poll with 60.3 per cent, with Lewis Hamilton second on 30.1 per cent and Charles Leclerc taking 6.9 per cent. Neither Lando Norris nor Oscar Piastri received a single vote.

The result reflects Russell's difficult recent form, with the Mercedes driver finishing only eighth at the United States Grand Prix last time out while teammate Antonelli took victory. Russell now sits just one point clear of Hamilton and six ahead of Verstappen with five rounds remaining.

The upgraded W17 has introduced a narrow and highly sensitive operating window that has proved difficult to set up consistently through race weekends.

Severe tyre degradation in dirty air during opening stints, combined with being stuck behind slower cars on identical power units, has worsened Russell's deficit to his teammate at recent events.

title: Lewis Hamilton responds to key F1 question: 'You've never had anyone like me here'
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has insisted that F1 has "never had anyone like me" before, as he fielded a question about his potential participation in the African Grand Prix.

Earlier this month, as revealed by RacingNews365 and then formally announced by F1, the championship will return to the continent of Africa for the first time since 1993 with a grand prix in Rwanda sometime in the next decade.

F1 is hopeful that the event, due to be held at a purpose-built track near the capital, Kigali, will host its first race in the "early 2030s", with seven-time champion Hamilton declaring previously that he would not retire from F1 until the series had raced in Africa.

As per the "early 2030s" timeline, Hamilton will turn 45 in January 2030, with old rival Fernando Alonso currently at that age, with the Spanish racer going to turn 46 midway through the 2027 season.

Hamilton, who is statistically the greatest driver of all time with 106 wins, 104 poles and 208 podiums to go with his seven titles, would be nearing 500 grands prix by the end of the 2030 season, if he does not take a sabbatical and starts every race between now and then.

Questioned whether he could make it to the first race in Rwanda, Hamilton was in a punchy mood ahead of his 399th F1 race.

"I mean, firstly, you've never had anyone like me here in the 70 years, so I feel that I'm built differently," Hamilton declared to media, including RacingNews365.

"Of course, there are challenges up ahead that I can't foresee that come with age, but along this way, along this journey, there have been so many preconceived ideas about the fact that your reaction time drops off.

"Did you see my reaction in the last race? My reaction is faster than some of the youngest people here, so there are lots of tools that you can utilise to continue to keep yourself and your mind sharp.

"I guess as long as you're willing to sacrifice everything, which I am right now. I can't say in four years whether I want to continue to do what I'm doing, but I love what I'm doing still now.

"I'm still all in, and I will be for the foreseeable future. Whether or not I can compete at 44 with a 20-year-old, who knows? But at 41, I can compete with a 20-year-old, so time will tell whether I'm here in the 2030s; we'll see."

[Article continues below]

'Not outstaying my welcome'

However, Hamilton did also add that he would not "outstay my welcome" - but pointed to his remarkable turnaround in form from his dreadful 2025 season at Ferrari.

For the first time in his then 19-year F1 career, Hamilton failed to score a grand prix podium as he struggled with the final ground effect Ferrari - but bounced back to take a first podium for the Scuderia in the Chinese GP, and then added his name to the drivers who had won for the team with victory in Barcelona.

"I never want to overstay my welcome in the sense of still not having the performance," he added.

"I don't want to be walking, driving around with that really dropping off, that my reactions have dropped off, that my driving has dropped off, and my pace has dropped off, which everyone has seen last year, but I proved everyone wrong with that, and I'll continue to try to do so."

title: Max Verstappen responds to Daniel Ricciardo Le Mans tilt: 'He's a smart man'
excerpt:
Max Verstappen, Daniel Ricciardo and Sebastian Vettel racing together at Le Mans? Not as crazy as it sounds!

Max Verstappen has responded to Daniel Ricciardo's suggestion that the pair team up with Sebastian Vettel for a crack at the 24 Hours of Le Mans, joking that his former Red Bull team-mate knows exactly what he is doing.

Ricciardo, who retired from F1 last year and now serves as a Ford Racing ambassador, floated the idea of an all-star endurance line-up with Verstappen and Vettel on a recent podcast appearance.

Speaking to media, including RacingNews365, Verstappen gave the idea a cautious welcome.

"He's a smart man to choose me in the car," quipped the four-time F1 champion.

"But we have to see. It just depends on a lot of things. For me, if I want to do it, I want to do it properly with really good prep.

"At the moment, I cannot do that. I don't have the free time to dedicate to a Le Mans project with all the other things that I'm doing outside of Formula 1."

Verstappen - 'A conversation already had'

The topic is not a fresh one for Verstappen, who revealed the subject has already come up in previous discussions with Ricciardo.

"It's not new to me, of course," confirmed Verstappen. "Yeah, we have spoken.

"From my side or his side, I don't think we are the types who always need to share everything, right? We talk about a lot of things in the background.

"But I think he has said it himself. He doesn't see himself coming back for a whole season. But the one-offs are interesting, and why not?

"But again, if we do something like that, and he will agree for sure, it needs to be proper, for a chance to win.

"And for a chance to win against people who do it for a whole season, you need to be really well prepared, so you just need to find the right timing."
